assessment.nobel_worthiness: Political economics (constitutions, electoral rules, state capacity, fiscal policy) built a unified theoretical and empirical framework that links political institutions to policy outcomes. It is broad in influence across public economics, development and comparative politics, and it follows naturally from recent institutions-and-growth recognition without duplicating it.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the central figures through their joint theory and empirical work on constitutions and electoral rules. Besley's work on state capacity and political incentives is closely complementary. A three-person grouping is coherent, though other political-economy theorists could reasonably be argued for.
assessment.maturity: The research programme spans about three decades with extensive replication, textbook treatment and policy influence. It is fully mature for recognition.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with the recent institutions-and-prosperity prize may weigh on timing.
Boundary between this work and adjacent political-economy contributions is somewhat fuzzy.
Causal identification in constitutional-effects empirics is debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting reshaped international trade theory and empirics, shifting the focus from countries and industries to firms and generating new welfare channels from trade. It has been very influential in applied work on trade, productivity and reallocation.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the canonical model and Helpman is the leading figure in the broader heterogeneous-firm and new trade theory programme, including work with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus FDI. Redding is a significant contributor but is a more marginal third name, so I propose two. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are notable empirical antecedents not on this entry, which creates some attribution tension.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation, and the framework is standard in graduate teaching and policy analysis.
uncertainties: Helpman also appears under a separate trade-politics entry, so a laureate choice must avoid double counting.
Priority questions regarding empirical antecedents.
Recognition of trade as a field may be viewed as already well served.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities underpins modern monetary policy analysis and central-bank practice, and its price-setting microfoundations are directly relevant to how firms adjust prices. Its importance to policy is very high.
assessment.attribution: Credit is diffuse. Calvo's staggered pricing, Taylor's rules and staggered contracts and Woodford's synthesis are distinct, while Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets contributed to empirical and DSGE implementation. A three-name limit forces a hard choice and leaves out many substantial contributors.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with decades of use in policy institutions. Parts of the framework were challenged after 2008 and during the 2021–23 inflation episode, though it has adapted.
uncertainties: Dispersed attribution across many scholars makes a clean laureate trio difficult.
Empirical performance of the framework in recent inflation episodes is contested.
Earlier recognition of related macroeconomists may affect the committee's appetite.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Law and finance opened a large research agenda on how legal origins and investor protection shape financial development, ownership structure and growth. It had broad influence across finance, law and development.
assessment.attribution: The core LLSV papers are tightly credited to Shleifer, La Porta and Lopez-de-Silanes. Vishny is a long-time collaborator mainly on separate corporate-governance work, so I omit him. Attribution to the core group is clearer than in most entries.
assessment.maturity: Well over two decades of citation and testing. However, the legal-origins thesis has been substantially critiqued on data coding, causal interpretation and persistence, and the empirical foundations are contested.
uncertainties: Robustness and causal interpretation of the legal-origins results remain contested.
Committee may weigh the critiques against the field-shaping impact.
Reputation issues surrounding one candidate may be relevant, though they are not assessed here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural estimation of differentiated-product demand and dynamic industry models gave empirical industrial organization a rigorous, widely used toolkit for market power, merger evaluation and welfare analysis. Its impact reaches antitrust practice and adjacent fields.
assessment.attribution: The BLP demand framework is clearly credited to Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. Pakes additionally contributed to dynamic games and the Ericson-Pakes framework, and Bresnahan, Reiss and others made foundational contributions on empirical market structure. The three-name choice is defensible but leaves out important contributors. As an IO-adjacent area it is close to my own field, so I have tried to apply the same criteria used for other fields.
assessment.maturity: BLP dates to the mid-1990s and is standard practice. Dynamic-model methods are somewhat less settled.
uncertainties: The cut between BLP and the dynamic or market-structure contributions is hard to draw.
Reliance on strong modelling assumptions and computational choices.
Possible perception that applied-methods recognition has recently been generous.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the China-shock evidence fundamentally changed understanding of how automation and trade reshape labour demand, wages and regional adjustment. It has high policy salience.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both the task framework (with Levy and Murnane) and the trade-shock work, and Hanson is central to the import-competition evidence. Dorn is a key coauthor on the China shock, and Katz is a pillar of the broader skill-biased technical change literature. Acemoglu's earlier recognition touches adjacent task theory, which complicates credit.
assessment.maturity: Two decades for task work and about a decade for the China shock. Replication and debate have so far supported the main findings in broad terms, though magnitudes are contested.
uncertainties: Overlap with themes already recognized in earlier prizes on technology and institutions.
Debate on magnitudes and persistence of the China-shock effects.
Choosing between the task and trade strands affects who is credited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Machine-learning methods for causal inference (double/debiased ML, causal forests, heterogeneous treatment effects) opened a new econometric toolkit with wide use in empirical economics, technology and policy evaluation.
assessment.attribution: Chernozhukov and coauthors developed double/debiased ML, while Athey and Wager developed causal forests and related heterogeneous-effects methods. Imbens, a laureate, and others contributed adjacent ideas. A two-name choice captures the broad leaders, but Wager's contribution is substantial and the credit is shared.
assessment.maturity: Roughly a decade old. Adoption is rapid, but long-run consolidation and the sorting of lasting from transient methods is incomplete.
uncertainties: Relatively recent, so lasting influence is not yet fully demonstrated.
Credit allocation among several close contributors.
Overlap with recent econometrics recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run top-income and wealth-distribution series, built from tax data, transformed measurement and public debate on inequality, and they motivated research in public economics and macroeconomics. Impact is very high, though some of it is in public discourse rather than in the theory.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the founders of the top-income data series and their joint analysis. Zucman's work on offshore wealth and distributional national accounts is a later, important extension. The choice among three is difficult, and I propose the two earliest originators.
assessment.maturity: The core data work is two decades old. Methodological critiques of capital-share interpretation and the wealth-tax implications remain unsettled.
uncertainties: Some conclusions, such as the dynamics of r versus g, are contested.
Weighing measurement contribution versus theoretical or causal contribution.
Saez also appears in another entry on optimal taxation, so a combined case is possible.
